mattress.overview: In most U.S. cities a mattress is bulky waste — not regular trash. The usual paths are scheduled curbside bulky/large-item pickup, a citizen drop-off station, or a paid hauler if you cannot wait for the city window.
prep_steps: Check whether your city uses a zone day, an appointment, or drop-off only.
Keep the mattress dry and clear of the cart path; wrap only if your city requires it for bed bugs.
Do not stuff a mattress into a standard trash cart — crews will leave it.
common_mistakes: Leaving it out on a non-bulky day (ticket or missed pickup).
Assuming every city picks up mattresses free every week — many cap volume or charge.
Mixing Freon appliances into the same pile when rules differ.

refrigerator.overview: Refrigerators contain refrigerant that cannot be vented. Cities either collect them on special bulky/appliance routes, require Freon removal and labeling first, or send you to a transfer station / licensed recycler.
prep_steps: Empty food and secure or remove doors for child safety where required.
Read your city guide for Freon rules before setting the unit at the curb.
Never cut lines or release refrigerant yourself.
common_mistakes: Taking a Freon appliance to an HHW site that rejects appliances.
Putting a fridge out with ordinary furniture bulk when Freon needs a separate call.
Assuming retailer haul-away is automatic — ask when you buy a replacement.

television.overview: TVs are usually e-waste, not garbage. Many cities ban them from landfill carts and offer free curbside e-waste days, transfer-station drop-off, or HHW/electronics events. CRT sets are the most restricted.
prep_steps: Confirm whether your city allows TVs on bulky day or only at an electronics site.
Wipe personal data from smart TVs when possible.
Check CRT rules — some resource centers refuse cathode-ray tubes.
common_mistakes: Putting a TV in the blue recycling cart.
Hauling a large TV to an HHW gate that only takes small electronics.
Ignoring appointment or item-count limits on free e-waste days.

paint-latex.overview: Latex (water-based) paint is often treated differently from oil-based paint. Many cities tell residents to dry latex solid for trash, while oil-based paint must go to HHW.
prep_steps: Identify the label — latex/acrylic vs oil-based/alkyd.
For latex: mix with cat litter or paint hardener until solid, then trash if your city allows.
For oil-based: keep the lid on and take it to HHW within local volume limits.
common_mistakes: Pouring paint down a drain or storm sewer.
Taking liquid latex to an HHW site that only wants oil-based products.
Leaving open cans at the curb as if they were bulky waste.

tires.overview: Passenger tires are rarely accepted in ordinary trash carts. Typical paths are a tire shop take-back, a county MMRF/transfer station limit (often rimless), or a city tire event.
prep_steps: Remove rims if your drop-off requires it.
Count your tires — many sites cap 4–5 per visit.
Skip curbside bulky unless your city explicitly lists tires.
common_mistakes: Leaving tires in an alley or vacant lot (illegal dumping).
Bringing commercial or agricultural tires to a residential-only event.
Assuming HHW accepts tires — most do not.

air-conditioner.overview: Window and portable AC units are Freon appliances. Treat them like refrigerators: city appliance routes, labeled Freon removal, or a transfer-station/recycler path — not a regular trash cart.
prep_steps: Keep the sealed system intact until a certified handler deals with refrigerant.
Follow your city Freon curb rules (doors/label/call-ahead).
Ask whether the unit counts toward bulky item limits.
common_mistakes: Venting refrigerant to make the unit ‘trash legal.’
Dropping an AC at HHW when appliances are banned there.
Setting it out on furniture-only bulk day.

lithium-battery.overview: Lithium-ion batteries are a fire hazard in garbage trucks and should never go in household trash or recycling carts. Use HHW, retailer take-back, or a battery drop program.
prep_steps: Tape the terminals or bag each battery separately.
Do not crush, charge, or store damaged batteries in a hot car.
Use your city HHW site or a listed battery collection partner.
common_mistakes: Tossing vape batteries or tool packs in the trash.
Mixing damaged lithium cells with alkaline household batteries unmarked.
Leaving a swollen battery in a device in the e-waste pile without flagging staff.

sofa.overview: Sofas and large upholstered furniture follow the same bulky channel as mattresses in most cities — scheduled pickup or drop-off, sometimes with cubic-yard caps.
prep_steps: Break down only if your city requires sections; many want items intact.
Keep the set-out clear of mailboxes, meters, and low wires.
Donate first if the piece is still usable and pest-free.
common_mistakes: Blocking the sidewalk or setting out days early.
Including contractor remodeling debris in a residential bulky pile.
Assuming a sleeper sofa with a metal frame is always recycling-week metal.

propane-tank.overview: Propane cylinders are hazardous and usually banned from trash carts and ordinary bulky piles. Grill-size tanks often go to HHW, exchange cages at retailers, or special collection events.
prep_steps: Do not puncture or put tanks in a garbage truck.
Check whether your HHW site takes 20 lb grill cylinders.
Use a retailer exchange for refillable tanks when available.
common_mistakes: Leaving a tank with furniture on bulky day.
Bringing large ASME/home tanks to a residential HHW that only takes small cylinders.
Throwing empty-looking cylinders in scrap metal without staff approval.
